title.en: Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing

headline.en: Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing: hear the whole song first, then the tune on its own.

detail.en: The whole song, every part together
The guide sings it, line by line
Stop if anything tightens or hurts

headline.en: Now the tune on its own.

detail.en: Follow the words as it plays

text.en: Find the notes of line 1: each one waits until you're on it.
Robert Robinson wrote the words when he was 22, in 1757 or 1758 (sources differ).

source.en: Wikipedia, "Come Thou Fount of Every Blessing"

text.en: Hear line 1, then sing it back.
Hear line 2, then sing it back.
Line 3 is the tune of line 1 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Line 4 is the tune of line 2 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Now lines 1 to 4 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
Hear line 5, then sing it back.
Hear line 6, then sing it back.
Line 7 is the tune of line 1 again, with new words. Sing it with the guide.
Hear line 8, then sing it back.
Now lines 5 to 8 joined: hear them, then sing them back.
The whole song, with the guide.
Sing your part with the other parts, and the guide with you. Hold your line while the others move.
The guide drops out: your part with the others only. Give me my note plays your first note quietly.
Once more on your own, from the top.
Record the tune of Come, Thou Fount of Every Blessing in Sing, with the other parts playing.

The tune first appears in John Wyeth's Repository of Sacred Music, Part Second, in 1813. It is named after the preacher Asahel Nettleton, and some credit him with it, but who wrote it is not known for sure.
